research_topic: Tribunus Compute Kernel: governed, copy-honest, Rust-native accelerator runtime — competitive landscape analysis, cross-backend zero-copy semantics, and architectural layering for local agentic compute
transcript_summary: A detailed architectural conversation exploring the design of a Tribunus Compute Kernel — a governed, copy-honest, Rust-native accelerator runtime for local agentic compute. The discussion covered the competitive landscape of existing projects (MLX, Burn, CubeCL, Candle, IREE, Arrow, DLPack), hardware-specific zero-copy semantics across Metal, CUDA, ROCm/HIP, and Intel oneAPI/SYCL, the three-layer architecture (data plane → execution plane → inference spine), the "copy honesty" doctrine over "universal zero-copy," positioning as a Tribunus subsystem integrated with the Runtime, Coordination Kernel, and Memory Spine, and backend sequencing (Metal first for Apple Silicon, then CUDA, ROCm/HIP, Intel, Vulkan/WebGPU).

research_findings.title: MLX: Apple Silicon Reference Architecture for Lazy Evaluation and Unified Memory
research_findings.finding: MLX is an Apple machine learning research framework where Core is C++ with Python, C, and Swift surfaces. Its key architectural advantages are: (1) lazy evaluation — computations build a graph and arrays materialize only when explicitly needed via eval(), item(), print(), or numpy conversion, giving the runtime room to fuse operations and avoid intermediate allocations; (2) unified memory on Apple Silicon — arrays reside in shared memory accessible by CPU and GPU without data copies; (3) Metal-backed kernel execution. MLX is not fundamentally Python; the Python API is a front-end over the MLX runtime. The important distinction is that zero-copy does not mean zero synchronization — ownership, hazard tracking, command-buffer fences, buffer lifetime discipline, and explicit materialization boundaries are still required.

research_findings.title: Burn + CubeCL: Rust-Native Portable GPU Compute (2026 State)
research_findings.finding: Burn is a Rust-native deep-learning framework. In 2026, Burn 0.20.0 (Jan 2026) introduced CubeK — a kernel-library layer built on CubeCL for high-performance multi-platform kernels (matmul, convolutions, attention, quantization, RNG). Burn 0.21.0 continued with significant framework-overhead improvements (fusion overhead down 5.4x average, peaking at 8.2x). CubeCL is the portable compute-kernel layer: a Rust language extension + JIT compiler + runtimes where a single #[cube] Rust-style kernel compiles to CUDA, HIP, Metal (via wgpu), Vulkan/SPIR-V, WebGPU/WGSL, and CPU SIMD. CubeCL is alpha but used in production by Burn. This maps directly to the multi-backend story Tribunus needs.

research_findings.title: Candle: Minimalist Rust ML Inference Framework
research_findings.finding: Candle (HuggingFace, v0.10.2) is a minimalist Rust ML framework with GPU support. It supports CPU, CUDA, and Metal as first-class Device variants. Features include safetensors loading via VarBuilder, Hugging Face model compatibility (LLaMA, Whisper, T5, YOLO, Segment Anything, Stable Diffusion, etc.), and WASM support. Candle is closer to lightweight inference substrate than governed runtime; its strongest GPU paths remain CUDA and Metal. For Tribunus, Candle is valuable as an inference-ergonomics reference rather than the architecture to adopt.

research_findings.title: IREE: MLIR-Based Compiler/Runtime for Heterogeneous Hardware
research_findings.finding: IREE (Intermediate Representation Execution Environment) is an MLIR-based end-to-end compiler and runtime that lowers ML programs through an MLIR pipeline to deploy across heterogeneous hardware (CPU, GPU, mobile, edge). It targets CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, and other backends via a unified IR. IREE is compiler/runtime infrastructure rather than an app-integrated local compute kernel, but its multi-backend IR lowering is directly relevant to Tribunus's need for portable execution without per-backend hand-coding.

research_findings.title: Apache Arrow C Data Interface: Zero-Copy Columnar Data Sharing
research_findings.finding: The Arrow C Data Interface enables zero-copy sharing of columnar data between independent runtimes in the same process using two C structs: ArrowSchema (type metadata) and ArrowArray (pointers to data buffers). Data is not copied; only addresses and metadata are transferred. A release callback manages resource lifetime. The Arrow C Device Data Interface extends this to GPU memory, enabling zero-copy sharing of device-resident data (used by RAPIDS cuDF). The interface is ABI-stable, has no external dependencies, and works via FFI with Rust, Python, Julia, and Go. For Tribunus, this is the model for zero-copy interchange between compute kernel, retrieval buffers, embeddings, and plugin consumers.

research_findings.title: DLPack: Cross-Framework Tensor Interchange Standard
research_findings.finding: DLPack (dmlc/dlpack) is an open in-memory tensor representation for zero-copy interchange between frameworks. It defines DLTensor (data pointer, device context DLContext with types like CPU/CUDA/OpenCL/ROCm/WebGPU, shape, strides, dtype, byte_offset) and DLManagedTensorVersioned (with deleter callback for lifetime). Adopted by PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, NumPy, CuPy, MXNet, TVM, PaddlePaddle. DLPack supports cross-hardware exchange including Metal, CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, WebGPU. Synchronization semantics for async GPU operations remain an active community discussion. For Tribunus, DLPack provides the canonical tensor interchange format for cross-framework and cross-plugin tensor sharing.

research_findings.title: CUDA Unified Memory, Pinned Host Memory, and Zero-Copy Semantics
research_findings.finding: NVIDIA CUDA (Programming Guide 13.3, May 2026) provides three memory strategies. Unified Memory (cudaMallocManaged, CUDA 6.0+): single coherent address space with automatic page migration between host and device, reduces explicit cudaMemcpy but has page-fault/migration overhead; cudaMemAdvise and cudaMemPrefetchAsync provide optimization hints. Pinned Host Memory (cudaMallocHost/cudaHostAlloc): page-locked host memory the GPU can access directly, enables fast async transfers (cudaMemcpyAsync), but is a scarce resource. Zero-Copy (cudaHostAllocMapped + cudaHostGetDevicePointer): GPU threads directly access host memory via mapped pinned buffers; ideal on integrated GPUs (Jetson) where CPU/GPU share DRAM; on discrete GPUs, interconnect bandwidth limits performance. For Tribunus: device-resident buffers plus explicit staging is the performant pattern for discrete GPUs; zero-copy via mapped pinned memory is a backend capability, not a default.

research_findings.title: ROCm/HIP: AMD Unified and Managed Memory (2026 State)
research_findings.finding: AMD HIP provides unified memory via hipMallocManaged with automatic page migration between host and device, similar to CUDA's model. __managed__ attribute for static allocations. On GPUs with HMM (Heterogeneous Memory Management) kernel support, standard malloc/new also work. hipMemAdvise and hipMemPrefetchAsync provide optimization hints. Supported on Vega+ GPUs on Linux. ROCm 7.2 (CES 2026) brought Windows support and Ryzen AI 400 Series support, signaling AMD's expanded investment. ROCm has undergone significant improvements since 2023. CUDA's unified memory is more mature, but HIP provides an open-source alternative with continuous improvement.

research_findings.title: Intel oneAPI/SYCL Unified Shared Memory (USM) and Level Zero
research_findings.finding: Intel SYCL USM provides three allocation types: malloc_device (device-only, fastest for kernels, requires explicit copy), malloc_host (host memory, accessible by device but accessed remotely via PCI-e, no explicit copy needed), malloc_shared (device-host shared, driver can dynamically migrate data, no explicit copies). Level Zero is the low-level direct-to-metal interface under oneAPI, providing explicit hardware control. SYCL buffers internally map to Level Zero USM allocations. In 2026, Intel removed sycl_ext_intel_usm_address_spaces, directing users to standard SYCL global_space. oneMKL 2026.0 supports system shared USM pointers on Linux. Integrated GPUs typically support USM directly.

research_findings.title: Apple Metal Storage Modes and Metal 4 (2026)
research_findings.finding: Metal provides four storage modes for buffers/textures. MTLStorageMode.shared: system memory accessible by CPU and GPU, default on Apple Silicon, ideal for CPU-GPU data sharing, leverages unified memory architecture (UMA) to eliminate copies — but developers must manage synchronization. MTLStorageMode.private: GPU-exclusive, allows Metal internal optimizations, suitable for render targets and GPU-generated intermediates; CPU population requires a shared→private blit. MTLStorageMode.managed: CPU and GPU maintain separate copies with explicit synchronization (didModifyRange), primarily for discrete GPU legacy, less relevant on Apple Silicon. MTLStorageMode.memoryless: on-chip tile memory, temporary render pass only. Metal 4 (2025) adds MTL4CommandAllocator for explicit memory management, placement sparse resources, unified command encoders, and direct Tensor compute kernel support.

research_findings.title: Safetensors: Safe, Zero-Copy Model Weight Serialization
research_findings.finding: Safetensors (HuggingFace, 2022) is a serialization format replacing pickle for ML model weights. Binary structure: 8-byte header size + JSON header (tensor names, shapes, dtypes, data_offsets) + contiguous data block (raw tensor bytes, C-order, little-endian, no compression). Key properties: (1) safe — strictly read-only, no arbitrary code execution unlike pickle; (2) zero-copy via mmap — tensor data mapped directly from disk into virtual address space; (3) lazy loading — only requested tensors/slices loaded on demand; (4) GPU copy still required but CPU-side allocation of all tensors can be bypassed. The format supports BF16/FP16 natively. For Tribunus, safetensors is the weight-loading format for the Inference Spine (Phase 3), enabling mmap'd model loading with lazy access.
